summary: Defines a YANG module for configuring named collections of trusted certificates and trusted public keys. Other data models can refer to these collections when they need to decide whom to trust. The module can also send notifications when certificates are about to expire.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a standard place, in a network device's configuration, to keep the certificates and public keys that the device trusts. The keys are held in named groups, so a setting such as a TLS client can say which group it wants instead of repeating the key data. The device can also send a notification when a certificate in the store is about to expire.

questions: how to configure a truststore with netconf
how does yang reference trusted certificates
subtitle: A standard YANG home for named bags of trusted certificates and public keys that other configuration can point to.

tldr.problem: Network devices are configured with trusted certificates and public keys, and the same key is often needed by several parts of the configuration. Without a shared place to keep them, every model carries its own copy, and nothing warns the operator that a certificate is about to expire.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9641 defines a YANG module named ietf-truststore that holds named bags of certificates and public keys, plus four reference types that let other modules point at a bag or at a single entry in the central truststore. Groupings let a model accept either a reference to a bag or a locally defined set of keys.
tldr.outcome: The module registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-truststore and the module name ietf-truststore at IANA. It also sends a certificate-expiration notification and keeps built-in trust anchors, which live in the operational datastore, separate from configured ones.

today: RFC 9641 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024, and it has not been obsoleted. IANA has registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-truststore and the YANG module name ietf-truststore with the prefix ts. The module is the second piece of a set whose first part, the crypto-types module, is RFC 9640.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9641 presents a YANG 1.1 module with five characteristics. It provides a central truststore for storing raw public keys and certificates. It supports named bags of raw public keys and named bags of certificates. It provides types that other data models can use to reference a raw public key or a certificate held in the central truststore. It provides groupings that let keys and certificates be configured inline or as references to truststore instances. And it lets the truststore be instantiated in other data models, in addition to or instead of the central truststore instance.

The document is compliant with the Network Management Datastore Architecture, so trust anchors installed during manufacturing, for instance for trusted well-known services, are expected to appear in the operational datastore rather than in the configuration.

Throughout the document the word central is used with truststore to refer to the top-level instance of the truststore grouping when the central-truststore-supported feature is enabled. Consuming modules may instantiate the same grouping in other locations, and those other instances are not the central one.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives network equipment a standard place to keep the keys and certificates it trusts. The keys are grouped into named sets, and other parts of the configuration can refer to a set by name instead of carrying their own copy. Equipment makers can also ship keys that are built in rather than configured.

sections.title: Relation to Other Modules
sections.content:
The module is part of a collection of RFCs that together support the configuration of both the clients and the servers of NETCONF and RESTCONF. The dependency diagram in the document draws its arrows from a referencer to the module it references. The crypto-types module, defined in RFC 9640, has no dependencies of its own, and the keystore module of RFC 9642 depends on it. The truststore module defined here depends on crypto-types, which supplies the groupings that describe how a certificate or a public key is stored.

The client and server modules for TCP, SSH and TLS all depend on the truststore module, as do the HTTP client and server module and the NETCONF and RESTCONF client and server modules. The TCP, SSH and TLS documents are published as RFCs 9643, 9644 and 9645; the HTTP, NETCONF and RESTCONF client and server documents are still works in progress at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: This module is one piece of a set. A base module supplies the format for storing a certificate or a key, this module holds the trusted ones, and the client and server modules for TCP, SSH, TLS and HTTP are built on top of it. The NETCONF and RESTCONF modules that read and write all of this sit underneath.

sections.title: Features, Typedefs and Groupings
sections.content:
The module defines four features. central-truststore-supported says the server implements the module and therefore supports the truststore. inline-definitions-supported says the server supports trust anchors defined locally. certificates says the server implements the certificate-bags subtree of the truststore, and public-keys says it implements the public-key-bags subtree.

It defines four typedefs, all of which extend the base leafref type: central-certificate-bag-ref, central-certificate-ref, central-public-key-bag-ref and central-public-key-ref. Each one is a path into the central truststore, so a consuming module can point at a named bag or at a single named entry inside a bag.

It defines five groupings. Two of them, central-certificate-ref-grouping and central-public-key-ref-grouping, offer a convenience way to configure a reference to a bag and to a single entry within it; the two leaves depend on each other, so neither can be set without the other. Two more, inline-or-truststore-certs-grouping and inline-or-truststore-public-keys-grouping, are choices: the keys are either defined inline in the configuration that uses them, or given as a reference to a bag in the central truststore. A server that wants truststore locations other than the central one augments its own case statements into those choices. The fifth grouping, truststore-grouping, defines the truststore itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The module has four optional capabilities a device can say it supports, four reference types that point into the truststore, and five reusable pieces of the model. Two of those pieces let another model point at a bag or at one key inside it. Two more let the model choose between writing the keys inline and pointing at a bag. The last one is the truststore itself, which other models may place wherever they need it.

sections.title: The Truststore Data Tree
sections.content:
The module's only protocol-accessible node is the container truststore, which is present only when the central-truststore-supported feature is enabled and which uses the truststore grouping. Because that grouping is defined separately from the protocol-accessible node, other modules can instantiate a truststore somewhere else in their own tree.

Inside the truststore are two containers, certificate-bags and public-key-bags, each present only if the matching feature is enabled. A certificate bag is a list keyed by name, with a name leaf, an optional description leaf and a list of certificates, each keyed by name and carrying the cert-data node defined by the crypto-types module. The cert-data node is a Cryptographic Message Syntax structure that can hold a chain of one or more certificates, and it is mandatory in the truststore. Each certificate also carries the certificate-expiration notification, which lets the server alert clients when a certificate is nearing expiration or has already expired. A public-key bag has the same shape, with a list of public keys, each carrying a name, a public-key-format identity and the key itself as binary data.

Every writable node in the module carries the NACM default-deny-write extension, so an access control model can restrict who is allowed to change the truststore.
sections.plainLanguage: The truststore holds two kinds of group, one for certificates and one for public keys. Each group has a name, an optional description and a list of entries, and each entry has its own name. Certificates are stored in the CMS format defined by the crypto-types module, and each one can report the date it expires. Public keys are stored with a format label and the key bytes.

sections.title: Example Usage
sections.content:
The examples are given in XML, as might be used with NETCONF; JSON can be used instead where RESTCONF is in use. The first example defines eight bags of trust anchors, four certificate bags and four public-key bags. The certificate bags cover trust anchor certificates for authenticating a set of remote servers, end entity certificates for authenticating a set of remote servers, trust anchor certificates for remote clients and end entity certificates for remote clients. The public-key bags cover SSH keys for remote servers, SSH keys for remote clients, raw public keys for remote servers and raw public keys for remote clients.

The descriptions in that example state how each bag is used. A server certificate is authenticated if its end-entity certificate has a chain of trust to one of the trust anchor certificates, and it is authenticated if the end-entity certificate is an exact match to one of the end entity certificates.

The second example shows the certificate-expiration notification for one of the configured certificates, naming the bag and the certificate and giving the expiration date. The third example illustrates the inline-or-truststore groupings with an example module. It gives two equivalent instances of each grouping, one referring to a bag in the truststore and one defining the same values inline. The two are equivalent because the inlined instance contains the same values as the truststore instance referenced by its sibling.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example fills a truststore with eight groups, four of certificates and four of public keys, separated by whether they are used for servers or for clients. It then shows how a device reports that one of those certificates is about to expire, and how another model can either point at a group or write the same values inline.

sections.title: Built-In Trust Anchors
sections.content:
Some implementations define built-in trust anchors. There may be built-in anchors that let the server connect securely to well-known services, such as a Secure Zero-Touch Provisioning bootstrap server, or public certification authority certificates for connecting to arbitrary web services using PKI.

Built-in trust anchors are expected to be set by a vendor-specific process, and any ability for operators to set or modify them is outside the scope of the document.

The defining characteristic of built-in trust anchors is that the server provides them rather than the configuration. They are therefore present in the operational datastore and in the system configuration, if implemented. In the example, the truststore bags that hold built-in anchors carry the origin annotation or:system, while the truststore itself carries or:intended.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices ship with keys already installed, such as the certificate for a well-known bootstrap service. Because the device supplies them rather than the configuration, they belong in the operational datastore, which holds state rather than configuration, and they are marked as coming from the system.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The name truststore suggests that its contents are protected from unauthorized modification. Controls for data in motion are described below, but controls for data at rest cannot be specified by a YANG module. To satisfy the expectations of a truststore, server implementations must ensure that the truststore contents are protected from unauthorized modification when at rest.

The module enables public keys to be configured without constraints on their usage, for instance whether a key may be used for encryption, for verification, or for both. Trust anchors configured this way are implicitly trusted to validate certification paths that may include any name, be used for any purpose, and be subject to no constraint imposed by an intermediate CA or by the context in which the truststore is used. Implementations are free to use alternative or auxiliary structures and validation rules that do limit how far a trust anchor applies.

The module defines groupings and containers designed to be reached over management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF, which have mandatory-to-implement secure transport layers such as SSH, TLS and QUIC, and mandatory-to-implement mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model provides the means to restrict a particular user's access to a preconfigured subset of the available operations and content.

Most of the readable data nodes in this module are not considered sensitive or vulnerable in network environments. The cert-data node is the exception: it uses the NACM default-deny-all extension. All the writable data nodes, both in the groupings and in the protocol-accessible truststore instance, may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, because a change to a trust anchor or to a reference to one can change the security policy of the device outright. For that reason the default-deny-write extension has been set for all data nodes defined in this module. The module defines no rpc or action statements, so no security considerations are given for those.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets two requirements. The device must protect the stored keys from being changed by anyone who is not allowed to change them, because a truststore others can edit is not a truststore. And a key added here is trusted for anything: it can validate any certificate name and serve any purpose, so a device that needs narrower rules has to add them itself. To help with that, every writable node in the module denies writes by default, and the certificate data itself denies reads by default.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has registered the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-truststore in the ns registry of the IETF XML registry, with the IESG as registrant contact.

IANA has also registered the YANG module ietf-truststore in the YANG Module Names registry, with that namespace, the prefix ts, and RFC 9641 as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA to register the module's XML namespace and the module name itself, so that other models can refer to it unambiguously. The prefix recommended for use in a configuration file is ts.

viz.caption: The modules that build on the truststore
The four features a device can announce

items.title: central-truststore-supported
items.text: The server implements the module and offers a truststore at the top level of its datastore.

items.title: inline-definitions-supported
items.text: The server supports trust anchors defined locally, next to the configuration that uses them.

items.title: certificates
items.text: The server implements the certificate-bags part of the truststore.

items.title: public-keys
items.text: The server implements the public-key-bags part of the truststore.

viz.caption: The nodes of the truststore container

root.label: truststore
root.note: Only present when the central-truststore-supported feature is enabled

children.label: certificate-bags
children.note: Present when the certificates feature is enabled

children.label: public-key-bags
children.note: Present when the public-keys feature is enabled

data.title: One certificate bag
data.code:
<truststore xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-truststore">
  <certificate-bags>
    <certificate-bag>
      <name>trusted-server-ca-certs</name>
      <description>
        Trust anchors (i.e., CA certs) used to authenticate server
        certificates.
      </description>
      <certificate>
        <name>Server Cert Issuer #1</name>
        <cert-data>BASE64VALUE=</cert-data>
      </certificate>
    </certificate-bag>
  </certificate-bags>
</truststore>
